blocks.text: In January 2026, the ghost of authoritarianism returned to roam and haunt Indonesian democracy. He did not bark through an open coup, but through the tidy political grip. Since the court, the early direction of Prabowo government shows a tendency to consolidate power that puts stability above quality, and loyalty above competence.

Niccoldore Machiavelli wrote, "It is much safer to be feared than loved." This principle feels alive in the Prabowo statement that's been told repeatedly, so I don't need a smart man, I need a loyal person. He found his concrete form in the early policy of government.

The superfat cabinet with representation of almost all political power is the most obvious example. On behalf of national unity, the opposition is practically disabled. This consolidation does create a short-term peace, but it disables control. John Stuart Mill once reminded us that bad institutions are those which do not allow the truth to be told.

Free Legizi Eating Policy, which is a superior program also reflects this pattern. The program was ambitious and popular, but was criticized for fiscal readiness, management, and budget priorities. Instead of opening up a data-based debate, the critics are often treated as disruption to a major agenda. Prosudular democracy is still going on, but substantial desertion is struck backwards by the narrative of loyalty and narrow nationalism.

On the other hand, expanding the role of a security officer in a civilian space through assignment and profiling a revised regulatory description strengthens the impression that the state is more comfortable relying on command discipline than the institutional capacity. Hannah Arendt writes, "Power and violence are options; where one rules absolutely, the other is absent."

Prabowo repeatedly claims he wants to build a strong country and carve out great history for Indonesia, and that he has a rare political capital, electrical legitimacy, parliament support and early stability. That golden opportunity should be used to uphold meritocracy, strengthen institutions, and allow critics to work as a democratic vitamin, not power toxins.

Indonesia is not the lack of a leader who wants to be feared, but always the lack of a leader strong enough not to fear differences, and the question is now, will the power built on fear be able to give birth to a gold history that is truly worth passing on to this nation?
